title: The AI office hype hasn't cleared, and the personal Agent war has already begun | Breaking down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
dek: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't even officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
why: Four frontline product people break down four routes — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. High information density, but the second half is worth more.
who: Product managers, investors and engineers watching AI application-layer startups, especially those building or preparing to build in the personal assistant direction who need to judge this round's valuation and product cadence.
skip: The 01:31 to 01:45 segment with the North American junior-year founder on the mic is mostly fundraising narrative, with information density clearly lower than the segments before and after.

points.h: 100,000 users prop up a $10 billion valuation
points.body: Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation went from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the new round being quoted in the market has already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old nobody, with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI — you can grab a ticket at the price of the next-generation personal operating system.

points.h: The line between tool and person is initiative
points.body: The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context re-explained every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are, like a friend or colleague; second, initiative — in Manus, setting up an automated task still depends on a prompt, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't initiative. True initiative is subjective agency — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and proactively comes over to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

points.h: Office Agents organise by project, personal Agents organise by person
points.body: The most core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centred on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks — it's office Agents that care a lot about task completion rate.

points.h: Town starts by trading email for the user's mandate
points.body: The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you hit confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate mandate bit by bit.

points.h: Poke didn't break out because of strategy, not technology
points.body: Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limit — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could absolutely have done it at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-mandate route, able to access credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it never took the step of "finishing the thing for you".

points.h: A cloud Agent has to handle three environments
points.body: Mark says doing a cloud agent was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

points.h: Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
points.body: Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like you paying for a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, a shopping guide, an agent — although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, and the scenarios they cut into and the users they filter out are different too.

points.h: For an Agent, your saved folder may be noise
points.body: The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was: extract what you like to eat from ingredients saved on Instagram, generate a shopping list, adjust the menu by dinner party headcount and dietary restrictions, then complete the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users close transactions is absolutely not in the top scenarios users want to solve; users more want to solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved folders — the truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

points.h: GUI is a maze map for ordinary people
points.body: Today didn't originally want to make a standalone app, and was very channel-heavy, integrating WeChat and Telegram, with most scenarios completed inside the channel. But it soon discovered the discoverability problem: users staring at a blank chat box had no idea what to do. So it had to step into GUI, and doing GUI requires a standalone app, and in the end it still made chat inside the app. Suki's takeaway is that GUI today no longer carries the user's operation entry point the way it used to, but is more like a map — to ordinary people an agent is more like a maze full of treasure, and GUI is giving ordinary people a map of the maze, along which you can discover the treasure.

points.h: If 90% of effort goes to generic capability, pivot
points.body: Suki originally made an AI education product, Monspeak, and when building 2.0 around Spring Festival this year discovered that to make a truly personalised teacher, 90% of the effort ended up going into how to make the agent run stably and have personalised memory. If 90% of the effort is going into a very generic capability, then conversely those generic Agents might eat the vertical scenario just by finishing it casually. So the judgment was that the consumer track won't end up with that many players — it will be highly concentrated, winner-take-all — and Suki switched to joining a startup to build personal AI together.

points.h: This wave has no network effect to lock users in
points.body: Suki believes this AI transformation is very different from the last mobile internet wave: the biggest change this wave is technological innovation, not the narrative of scaling up, burning money and building network effects. There is no network effect or scale effect that can lock users in — as long as your product is good, I'll switch to another product the very next day, because no two-sided network platform has formed, and there's no reason users must stay with you. People stay on Xiaohongshu and Douyin because a two-sided network platform has formed, and they can't easily migrate away. So innovative companies are actually easier to fight than in the last mobile internet wave — just hurry to innovate and win users with the best experience.

points.h: The most valuable thing is that middle processing layer
points.body: At the end they asked where the most valuable position is in the personal agent era. Suki picks trust and habit — context is only the entry-level foundation; ultimately it's the dependence, habit and trust formed through long-term use; if forced to choose, it leans toward the end closer to the user, because model makers are still chasing each other, and the merchant and MCP end will grow naturally with the market. Mark thinks it's neither context nor the ecosystem layer: just getting a lot of context is not nearly enough, it doesn't directly deliver value, and memory is far more complex than imagined — something said last week may already be invalid this week, and still sitting in memory is serious noise. The most valuable thing is that middle processing layer, a bit like Douyin's recommendation algorithm; how the execution mechanism works is each company's secret.

terms.def: An AI that organises context around the user themselves, understands you long-term and proactively does things for you.
The engineering layer that wraps the model and is responsible for calling tools and completing tasks.
An open protocol ecosystem that lets AI call external tools and data.
The ability for AI to operate web pages through the browser interface on a person's behalf.
The general ability for AI to directly control a graphical interface to complete tasks.
The information about you that AI can see, including history, preferences and the current task.
